data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

A common misconception is that Earth’s shadow causes ordinary phases. Test that idea with a teacher-supervised cool LED lamp and ball on a blunt handle. Keep the ball out of your head shadow near full phase; never use the Sun or a laser.

1. Read **Moonlight and Changing Views** — compare illumination, viewing angle and eclipses.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Keep the **One Ball, One Lamp** chart open while you work.
4. Sort the cards in **Phase or Eclipse?** — explain the evidence for each choice.
5. Take the quiz. Question 3 is the shadow trap.
6. Explain a phase to someone at home using the **Sentence Frames**.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember Moonlight and Changing Views** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Moon Model That Cannot Fool Anyone** — build the model, and mark every guess as a guess.

Bonus: look at the real Moon tonight and name its phase before you check. 🌙

Picture panels: Illumination and phase sequence; Growing and shrinking visible light; Two different eclipse alignments; Rotation and a classroom model. Images are text-free with editable captions. Distinguish Earth-view phase disks from space-view position diagrams: orbit pictures show the Sun-facing hemisphere, not the phase seen from Earth. Right-lit waxing examples use a northern-up textbook convention; viewing orientation varies with location and time. Dark outlines make the new Moon’s position visible in diagrams, not in the real night sky. All sizes, distances, shadow cones and orbital planes are simplified and not to scale. Lunar surface textures are artistic. Ordinary phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow. Keep the model ball out of the observer’s head shadow for a full phase; deliberately align it only when demonstrating an eclipse. Use a cool lamp and blunt handle with teacher supervision, never direct solar viewing or a laser. Educator review remains pending.

history.data:
## Moonlight and Changing Views

Outside a lunar eclipse, approximately half of the Moon receives sunlight. The Moon is a sphere: its Sun-facing hemisphere is illuminated, while its other hemisphere has night. A phase describes how much of the illuminated hemisphere we see from Earth, not how much of the entire Moon receives sunlight.

As the Moon orbits Earth, our viewing angle changes. At new moon, the Moon is in the Sun's direction and its illuminated hemisphere faces mostly away from us. At first quarter, roughly a week later, half of the visible disk is illuminated. At full moon, the Moon is opposite the Sun in our sky and we see its illuminated face. Third quarter shows the other half disk. A crescent has less than half of its visible disk illuminated; a gibbous has more than half but less than all. Waxing means that visible illuminated fraction is growing toward full; waning means it is shrinking toward new.

The phase cycle averages 29.5 days. The Moon orbits Earth and rotates once in about 27.3 days relative to distant stars. The phase cycle is longer because Earth and the Moon also travel around the Sun: the Moon must move farther to reach the same Sun-Earth-Moon angle again.

Ordinary phases are not caused by Earth's cast shadow. The boundary between the Moon's own day and night is called the terminator. Model phases with a cool LED lamp and a ball on a blunt handle, under teacher supervision. Hold the ball at arm's length and turn to change the viewing angle. Near full moon, hold it slightly above your head's shadow so your body does not cause an accidental eclipse. Keep the ball out of that shadow unless you deliberately demonstrate an eclipse. Never use direct solar viewing or a laser for this activity.

A lunar eclipse happens at full moon when the Moon enters Earth's shadow. It can be penumbral, partial or total. During totality the Moon often looks copper red because sunlight filtered and bent through Earth's atmosphere reaches it. A lunar eclipse can be observed where the Moon is above the horizon and weather permits.

A solar eclipse happens at new moon when the Moon blocks some or all of the Sun for observers in the affected part of Earth. A total eclipse has a narrow path of totality, with a wider region seeing a partial eclipse. An annular eclipse leaves a bright ring because the Moon appears too small to cover the Sun completely. Never look directly at the Sun during this classroom investigation.

Eclipses do not happen every month. The Moon's orbital plane is tilted about five degrees to Earth's orbital plane around the Sun. Most new and full moons miss the necessary alignment; eclipses require alignment near where those planes cross. Our flat diagrams omit that tilt and are not to scale.

The Moon rotates once per orbit, so approximately the same face stays toward Earth. Small apparent rocking motions, called libration, let us see a little around its edges over time. The far side is not permanently dark. Phase pictures can appear rotated with viewing location and time; our right-lit waxing examples use a northern-up textbook convention.

cards.target: Lunar eclipse at full moon, solar eclipse at new moon, and why they are rare
essentialFacts: At a lunar eclipse the full Moon enters Earth’s shadow; totality often looks reddish, while partial and penumbral eclipses differ.
A solar eclipse happens when the new Moon casts its shadow on a small part of Earth.
The Moon’s orbital plane is tilted about five degrees to Earth’s orbital plane, so most new and full moons miss the alignment.
cards.aiExample: LUNAR eclipse: the Moon is the one in the dark, so it must be FULL and behind Earth. SOLAR eclipse: the Sun is the one blocked, so the Moon must be NEW and in front. Lunar-full-behind; solar-new-in-front. And TILT is why it is rare.
cards.mapping: Each eclipse is hooked to the thing that goes dark: the Moon (lunar) or the Sun (solar). Knowing what goes dark tells you the phase and the position, and the keyword tilt carries the rarity rule.

questions.question: Outside a lunar eclipse, approximately how much of the whole Moon receives sunlight?
options: It depends on the phase: a sliver during a crescent, all of it when full
Approximately half, the hemisphere facing the Sun
All of it, but Earth's shadow hides part of it from us
Only the side that faces Earth, since that side never changes
questions.correctAnswer: Approximately half, the hemisphere facing the Sun

questions.question: Why does the Moon look like a full circle one week and a half circle a week later?
options: The Moon spins faster during some weeks than others
Clouds high in Earth's atmosphere cover part of the Moon
Earth's shadow slides across the Moon and back each month
The Moon moved along its orbit, so we see the lit half from a new angle
questions.correctAnswer: The Moon moved along its orbit, so we see the lit half from a new angle

questions.question: A friend says the crescent Moon is 'Earth's shadow covering most of the Moon.' What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing is wrong; Earth's shadow makes every phase
Earth’s cast shadow causes lunar eclipses, not ordinary phases
Earth's shadow is too small to cover more than a sliver of the Moon
The crescent is caused by the Sun's shadow, not Earth's
questions.correctAnswer: Earth’s cast shadow causes lunar eclipses, not ordinary phases

questions.question: During which phase can a lunar eclipse happen, and why?
options: New moon, because the Moon is closest to the Sun then
First quarter, because half the Moon is already dark
Full moon, because the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun
Any phase, because eclipses depend on weather rather than position
questions.correctAnswer: Full moon, because the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun

questions.question: Why is there NOT a lunar eclipse every month at full moon?
options: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below Earth's shadow
Earth's shadow is only long enough to reach the Moon a few times a year
The Moon moves too fast to stay in the shadow long enough to darken
Eclipses only happen in years when the Moon is closest to Earth
questions.correctAnswer: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below Earth's shadow

questions.question: How can a cool lamp and ball show that ordinary phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow? Include how you avoid an accidental model eclipse.
questions.expectedAnswer: With teacher supervision, use a cool LED lamp, a ball and a blunt handle. Hold the ball at arm’s length and turn to see a crescent, half disk and full disk as the viewing angle changes. Lift the ball slightly above the observer’s head shadow near full phase. Deliberately moving it into that shadow models a lunar eclipse instead. Never use the Sun or a laser.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a lunar eclipse and a solar eclipse: whose shadow, which phase, and who can see it.
questions.expectedAnswer: A lunar eclipse occurs at full moon in Earth’s shadow; it is visible where the Moon is above the horizon and weather permits. Total lunar eclipses often look red, but partial and penumbral eclipses also occur. A solar eclipse occurs at new moon when the Moon blocks the Sun for affected observers on Earth. Totality occupies a narrow path, with partial views over a wider region.

reflections.text: What did you believe about the Moon's phases before this lesson? What changed your mind?

data.question: Why can I sometimes see the Moon in the daytime? ☀️🌙
data.answer: The Moon can be above the horizon during daylight and bright enough to see against the sky. Visibility depends on phase, location, time and conditions. First-quarter Moon is often visible in the afternoon, and third-quarter Moon in the morning.

data.question: Is there really a dark side of the Moon?
data.answer: The far side mostly faces away from Earth, but it receives sunlight too. The Moon’s own night moves around it. Libration lets us see a little around the edges over time; far side does not mean permanently dark.

data.question: Why does the Moon look orange or huge near the horizon? 🍊
data.answer: Near the horizon, moonlight passes through more air, which scatters away more blue light and can leave an orange appearance. The striking increase in apparent size is mainly a perceptual illusion. Its angular size changes little during that short rise, though Earth-Moon distance changes its actual angular size over an orbit.

data.question: Do phases look the same in Australia?
data.answer: Observers see essentially the same phase at the same time, but it can appear rotated with location and time. Northern and southern views often have opposite orientations. Right-lit does not universally mean waxing; follow the illuminated fraction across successive days.

data.question: Why is a total solar eclipse such a big deal if it only lasts a few minutes? 🌑
data.answer: Totality crosses a narrow path, so any particular location experiences it infrequently. The interval varies greatly by location. A wider surrounding region can see a partial solar eclipse.

data.question: Does the Moon really pull the ocean?
data.answer: Yes. The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans, and that pull is the main cause of tides. It is a different lesson, but it is the same Moon doing the work.

data.title: A Moon Model That Cannot Fool Anyone
data.instructions: Design and test a model that distinguishes ordinary phases from Earth’s cast shadow and shows the alignments needed for eclipses.
data.fitReason: The lesson's core skill is using a model to explain a cyclic pattern, which is exactly the NGSS performance expectation. Designing the model for a skeptical younger audience forces students to make the geometry visible, not just described.

brief.context: A younger class is investigating whether Earth’s shadow causes ordinary phases. Design a demonstration under ten minutes using teacher-supervised cool LED lamps, foam balls of two sizes, blunt handles, string, a globe and cardboard. Keep room lighting comfortable. Do not use direct solar viewing or lasers.
brief.audience: A fourth-grade class and their teacher
brief.drivingQuestion: How can we build and run a model that makes a fourth grader see, without being told, that phases come from viewing angle, and that eclipses need a special lineup that usually does not happen?
brief.seedDirection: Decide first who plays Earth. The person watching from Earth's position is the one who sees the phases, so the model has to be run from that viewpoint.
lockedLessonFacts: Outside lunar eclipses, approximately half of the Moon receives sunlight.
Phases are the angle from which we see the lit half as the Moon orbits Earth; Earth's shadow is not the cause.
A lunar eclipse happens when the full Moon passes through Earth's shadow; a solar eclipse happens when the new Moon's shadow falls on Earth.
The Moon’s orbital plane tilts about five degrees to Earth’s orbital plane, so eclipses do not occur every month.
One rotation per orbit keeps approximately the same face toward Earth; libration reveals some edges.
openQuestions: How far from the lamp does the ball need to be so the lit half is clearly half, not a glare?
How do we show the five-degree tilt in a model a fourth grader can hold?
What will fourth graders predict before we run it, and how do we let them test their prediction?
How big should the Moon ball be compared to the Earth globe for the shadows to work?
stakeholders: The fourth graders who currently believe the shadow idea
Their teacher, who needs the model to fit in ten minutes
Anyone with light sensitivity in a dark room
criteria: A fourth grader standing at Earth's position can name the phase they see at four points around the orbit
The model shows a full-moon position where Earth's shadow misses the Moon and one where it hits
Fourth graders write a prediction before the demo and check it after
The script uses four glossary words correctly and distinguishes the Moon’s own night from Earth’s cast shadow
constraints: Runs in under ten minutes including setup
Teacher-supervised cool LED lamps and blunt handles only; no direct solar viewing or lasers
Must work in a classroom that cannot be made fully dark
brief.deliverable: A labeled diagram of the model, a ten-minute demonstration script with the prediction step marked, a test log from running it once with your own class, and a one-paragraph note on what your model cannot show.

parallelExample.context: A planetarium educator kept hearing visitors say the crescent is Earth's shadow.
parallelExample.move: An educator asks learners to turn while holding balls at arm’s length beside a lamp. Near full phase they lift each ball slightly above their head shadow. They compare that bright full view with a deliberate move into the shadow, which produces a model eclipse.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Comparing the two positions separates ordinary changing views from an actual cast shadow. The observer’s shadow must be managed, not assumed absent.

supports.frameStarter: In our model, ____ is the Sun, ____ is the Moon, and ____ stands where Earth is. When the Moon ball is at ____, the person at Earth sees ____.
frameChoices: Each fourth grader holds their own Moon ball and turns under one lamp
One large model at the front with a volunteer standing at Earth
A ring of eight balls fixed around a globe showing all phases at once
A tilted hoop for the orbit so the eclipse lineup is visible
coachPrompts: At full phase, is the ball above the observer’s head shadow? What changes when you deliberately lower it into that shadow?
Which criterion is hardest to meet in a room that is not dark?
What would a fourth grader still get wrong after your model, and can you fix that or only name it?
